lessons.title: Living and non-living things
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: List the seven characteristics of living things.
Sort things into living, non-living and once-living.
Explain why a car or a river is not a living thing.
reviewNotes: Whether fire and viruses count as living is not discussed; keep to the classic classification. MRS GREN word list should match the syllabus wording.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Living things
blocks.md: All **living things** do seven things (remember MRS GREN): **M**ove, **R**espire (breathe), be **S**ensitive (feel and react), **G**row, **R**eproduce (have young), **E**xcrete (get rid of waste) and take in **N**utrition (food). Plants, animals and tiny living things like bacteria are all living. Stones, water, plastic and cars are **non-living**.

blocks.caption: The seven characteristics of living things.
blocks.alt: Seven boxes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition, each with a short explanation.

blocks.title: Once-living things
blocks.md: Some things are not alive now but **were** alive: dry wood, a dead leaf, a bone, cotton cloth and leather. We call them **once-living** (or dead) things. A thing that is alive must show **all** seven signs, not only one: a car moves but it does not grow, feed or reproduce, so it is non-living.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that a thing is alive because it **moves** (a car, a river, the wind).
- Saying that plants are not alive because they do not move from place to place: they grow, feed, reproduce and react to light.
- Forgetting that seeds are alive: they are resting and can grow when they get water and warmth.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Sort into living, non-living and once-living: a goat, a stone, a dry leaf.
steps: A goat moves, breathes, feeds, grows and has young: living.
A stone does none of these: non-living.
A dry leaf came from a plant that was alive: once-living.
blocks.answer: goat: living; stone: non-living; dry leaf: once-living.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why is a motorbike not a living thing?
steps: It moves, but only when someone starts it with fuel.
It does not grow, reproduce, breathe or react like a living thing.
blocks.answer: A motorbike moves, but it does not grow, breathe, feed or reproduce, so it is not alive.

lessons.title: Plants: parts and their jobs
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the main parts of a flowering plant and say what each part does.
Explain how a green plant makes its food.
Give examples of plant parts that we eat.
reviewNotes: Cassava is described as a root (storage root); yam/cocoyam are left out as botanical classification is more complex. Photosynthesis is simplified.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Parts of a plant
blocks.md:
- **Roots**: hold the plant in the soil and take in water and minerals.
- **Stem**: holds up the plant and carries water and food up and down.
- **Leaves**: make food for the plant.
- **Flower**: makes seeds.
- **Fruit**: grows from the flower and protects the seeds.
- **Seeds**: can grow into new plants.

blocks.caption: The parts of a flowering plant.
blocks.alt: A drawing of a plant. Below the ground line are the brown roots. A green stem rises from the ground with two leaves and a pink flower on top. The parts are labelled flower, leaf, stem and roots.

blocks.title: How a plant makes food
blocks.md: A green plant makes its own food in its leaves. This is called **photosynthesis**. The leaf uses **sunlight**, **water** (from the roots) and **carbon dioxide** (from the air) to make food (sugar), and it gives out **oxygen**. Because plants make food, they are the first link in every food chain: they are **producers**.

blocks.title: Plant parts we eat
blocks.md:
- Roots: cassava, carrot.
- Stem: sugar cane.
- Leaves: eru, bitter leaf, cabbage.
- Fruits: mango, tomato, pawpaw.
- Seeds: maize, beans, groundnuts, rice.
A balanced diet uses several of these.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that plants feed on soil. They take **water and minerals** from the soil, but they make their **food** in the leaves.
- Thinking that photosynthesis happens at night: it needs light.
- Mixing up the stem (holds the plant) and the roots (take in water).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for two weeks. It becomes pale and weak. Explain why.
steps: Leaves make food by photosynthesis, and this needs sunlight.
In the dark the plant cannot make food, so it becomes pale and weak.
blocks.answer: Without sunlight the leaves cannot make food, so the plant becomes pale and weak.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Name the part of the plant that we eat in: cassava, eru, maize.
steps: Eru is a leaf. Maize grains are seeds.
blocks.answer: cassava: root; eru: leaves; maize: seeds.

lessons.title: Animals and their habitats

objectives: Sort animals into vertebrates and invertebrates.
Name the five groups of vertebrates and one feature of each.
Say where some animals live (habitats) and what they eat.
reviewNotes: The animals named are common in Cameroon; classifications (bat, whale, spider) are standard textbook facts.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Vertebrates and invertebrates
blocks.md: **Vertebrates** have a backbone. **Invertebrates** have no backbone. Vertebrates: **mammals**, **birds**, **reptiles**, **amphibians** and **fish**. Invertebrates include insects, spiders, snails, worms and crabs. Most animals on Earth are invertebrates.

blocks.caption: Groups of animals with examples.
blocks.alt: Six boxes: mammals (goat, human), birds (hen, eagle), reptiles (lizard, snake), amphibians (frog, toad), fish (tilapia, catfish) and invertebrates (ant, snail).

blocks.title: The five groups of vertebrates
blocks.md:
- **Mammals**: have hair or fur, give birth to live young and feed them milk (goat, human, bat).
- **Birds**: have feathers and wings, lay eggs with hard shells (hen, eagle).
- **Reptiles**: dry scaly skin, most lay eggs (lizard, snake, crocodile).
- **Amphibians**: moist skin, young live in water and adults on land and in water (frog).
- **Fish**: live in water, breathe with gills, have fins and scales (tilapia).

blocks.title: Habitats and feeding
blocks.md: A **habitat** is the place where an animal lives: forest, savanna, river, sea, soil, a pond. Animals that eat only plants are **herbivores** (goat, cow); animals that eat other animals are **carnivores** (lion, snake); animals that eat both are **omnivores** (human, chicken). An insect has **6 legs** and 3 body parts; a spider has **8 legs**, so a spider is not an insect.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that a bat is a bird because it flies: it has fur and feeds its young with milk, so it is a mammal.
- Saying that a whale or a dolphin is a fish: they are mammals.
- Saying that all animals that live in water are fish: a frog is an amphibian.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Say which group of animals each belongs to: a frog, a hen, a goat.
steps: A frog has moist skin and lays eggs in water: amphibian.
A hen has feathers and wings: bird.
A goat has hair and feeds its kids with milk: mammal.
blocks.answer: frog: amphibian; hen: bird; goat: mammal.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A creature has 8 legs and no backbone. Is it an insect?
steps: Insects have 6 legs. This animal has 8 legs.
It has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate, but it is not an insect (it is like a spider).
blocks.answer: No. It is an invertebrate with 8 legs, like a spider.
